report:
Your skepticism is understandable, but the evidence points the other way: for **pharmaceutical-grade, purified cannabidiol (Epidiolex) as add-on therapy**, randomized trials show reduced **convulsive** seizure frequency in pediatric Dravet syndrome.

In the pivotal double-blind RCT (120 patients, ages 2–18), median monthly convulsive seizures fell from 12.4 to 5.9 with CBD vs 14.9 to 14.1 with placebo; median reduction was about 39% vs 13%, adjusted difference 22.8%, p=0.01. Adverse events were more common with CBD. https://resident360.nejm.org/content-items/trial-of-cannabidiol-for-drug-resistant-seizures-in-the-dravet-syndrome-3

A later dose-ranging RCT found adjunctive CBD 10 or 20 mg/kg/day produced greater convulsive-seizure reductions than placebo, supporting a dose-response relationship. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7052786/

Regulatory labeling reflects this: FDA states Epidiolex’s Dravet effectiveness was demonstrated in a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of 120 patients aged 2–18 using 20 mg/kg/day. https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2018/210365lbl.pdf

Open-label extension data suggest benefit can persist, though uncontrolled long-term evidence is weaker and safety monitoring matters—especially liver enzymes with valproate and interactions with clobazam. https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/epi.17036

**Conclusion:** the claim is broadly supported for prescription CBD; it should not be generalized to artisanal/over-the-counter CBD products.
